attached.title: A module is a program unit identifiable through compiling, combining, and loading processes.
Modules are logically separable parts of a program, focusing on discrete functionalities. Functions and routines should be logically separable if placed in distinct modules.
Modules represent a collection of source code files managed separately in the build process. This definition emphasizes the structuring and handling of files within the software engineering context.
A module consists of data, functions, and routines operating on that data. This definition aligns closely with the concept of a class in object-oriented programming, combining data and behavior.
Once software is modularized, changes can be made more easily. Modules can be reused in other software, providing two types of flexibility.
Breaking a program into modules enhances understanding. Each module can be comprehended individually, leading to a clearer understanding of the program as a whole.
Discrete development of each program section by different teams can shorten the life cycle. Working with modules is more efficient than working on a monolithic codebase.
Software complexity can be measured using metrics such as excessive cyclomatic interaction
Comprehensibility is a key aspect of modularity
Software should be designed for easy understanding and future adaptability
Associated with excessive difficulty in understanding
Module cohesion is a way to reason about the contents of a single module, focusing on the relationships between its elements.

There are different ways for the elements to relate; for example, they might be functions that work on the same type of data or the program might execute the function at a similar point in time. Some of these are desirable, others are not.
The manner and degree to which tasks in a module are related to each other.
A measure of the strength of the relationship between items within a module.
All parts of the module perform a single well-defined task.
Enhances modularity, makes the module's purpose clear, improves maintainability.
Modules working together towards a specific defined goal.
Elements operate on the same data or are involved in the same task.
Reduces coupling and promotes better organization within the module.
Combining modules that operate on the same inputs and outputs.
The output of one part is the input to another, forming a pipeline.
Useful in stream processing but can be less flexible.
Elements contribute to a series of steps in a procedure.
Weaker than functional cohesion; related by sequence rather than function.
Parts of a procedure placed together without necessarily working on the same data.
Elements perform similar activities as dictated by some controlling logic.
Can become complex and harder to maintain.
Modules doing similar things but not directly related, e.g., different cases in a switch statement.
Elements involved in activities related in time.
Can lead to a module doing too many unrelated tasks.
Modules grouped by the timing of operations, such as startup or cleanup routines.
No meaningful relationship between the elements; they are just grouped together.
Leads to confusion and maintenance difficulties.
Modules with unrelated functions grouped together.
The manner and degree of interdependence between software modules. Coupling indicates how closely connected different modules are and how much they rely on each other.
Two modules rely on each other to perform certain tasks. This dependency can be one-way or mutual.
How one module relies on another. For example, a module providing mathematical functions that another module uses for computation.
The number of points of reliance between modules, indicating the extent of their interdependence.
How much impact modules have on each other. For instance, whether they simply pass data or deeply collaborate to change the program state.
A module passing parameters to another versus two modules jointly managing application state.

The directness of the interaction between modules. For example, if Module 1 interacts with Module 2 and Module 3 also interacts with Module 2, then Module 1 and Module 3 are indirectly connected through Module 2.
Three modules where the first and third interact via the second, indicating a more distant but still relevant connection.
This definition summarizes the previous aspects, indicating how closely connected and interdependent the modules are within a program.
Evaluating the overall dependencies in a software system to determine how changes in one module might affect others.
Desirable in software design. Modules with low coupling are easier to maintain, test, and reuse because changes in one module have minimal impact on others
Generally undesirable as it makes the system more complex and harder to maintain. High coupling increases the risk of ripple effects where changes in one module necessitate changes in others.
Define clear interfaces for modules to interact, reducing direct dependencies.
Using abstract classes or interfaces in object-oriented programming to define common behaviors without specifying the implementation.
Encapsulate module details and expose only what is necessary. This limits the impact of changes to the internal workings of a module.
Using private methods and properties in classes to hide implementation details.
Inject dependencies rather than hardcoding them within modules. This promotes flexibility and easier testing.
Using a dependency injection framework in a language like Java or .NET.
Modules communicate through events, reducing direct dependencies.
Using an event bus or message queue to decouple modules in a microservices architecture.
Makes modules dependent on the environment they share.
One module accesses the internals of another.
Makes modules dependent on each other's implementation.
One module accessing the data of another.
One module controls the behavior of another.
Makes modules dependent on the control flow of another.
One module passing control information to another.
Modules interact by passing data between them (input-output coupling)
Makes modules dependent on the data they share.
Modules passing data to each other.
Makes modules dependent on global state.
A combination of different types of coupling.
Makes modules dependent on multiple aspects of each other.
Modules sharing global data and passing control information.
Modules share a composite data structure.
Makes modules dependent on the structure of shared data.
Modules sharing a struct or class.
Makes modules independent of each other's implementation.
Modules are dependent on each other in a way that is difficult to understand.
Makes modules difficult to maintain and understand.
